title: “The truth has been hidden from you”: the spiritual blindness appeal
excerpt: When arguments do not persuade, some Christian writers tell Muslims they cannot see the truth because their minds have been blinded. The appeal can be made by any faith against any other, which is why it settles nothing.
content:
One page published alongside the Islamic Dilemma is addressed directly to Muslims. “If you are in Islam,” it begins, “I believe the truth has been hidden from you.” It goes on to explain, from several New Testament passages, that Satan blinds the minds of unbelievers so they cannot see the light of the gospel, and that God allows this blindness as a judgment on those who keep rejecting Him.

Muslims who read it are told, in effect, that if they remain unpersuaded, it is because something is wrong with their sight.

What the page says

The page quotes four groups of passages. “The god of this age has blinded the minds of unbelievers, so that they cannot see the light of the gospel” 2 Cor 4:4 · NIV.

“He has blinded their eyes and hardened their hearts” John 12:40 · NIV. The warnings in Hebrews against hardening one’s heart and against falling away.

And Paul’s description of people whose “foolish hearts were darkened” because they refused to honour God (Romans 1:21). It ends with advice: pray, read the Gospels, do not harden your heart.

The advice at the end is good advice for anyone, and we return to it below. The problem is with the frame around it.

An appeal any faith can make

The first thing to notice about the spiritual blindness appeal is that it is symmetrical. The Qur’an has its own language of sealed hearts and unseeing eyes.

It speaks of those on whose hearts and hearing God has set a seal, and over whose eyes is a covering Q 2:7. It describes people who “have hearts with which they do not understand, eyes with which they do not see, and ears with which they do not hear” Q 7:179. A Muslim could quote these verses to a Christian with exactly the same confidence the page quotes Paul to Muslims.

When both sides can make the same appeal with equal sincerity, the appeal cannot decide between them. It tells us that each side believes the other is missing something, which we already knew.

It does not tell us which side is right. For that, the Qur’an says, there is only one test: “Say: bring your proof, if you are truthful” Q 2:111.

An appeal that cannot be tested

The second problem is that the appeal is unfalsifiable. If a Muslim is persuaded by the Islamic Dilemma, that shows the argument is sound.

On this logic, a Muslim who stays unpersuaded is blind. There is no outcome in which the argument could be found weak, because every failure to persuade is explained in advance as a fault in the listener.

That is a comfortable position, but it is not a rational one, and it is not respectful. It means the argument’s advocates never have to ask whether their reading of Q 5:47 is mistaken, or whether the Qur’an’s Injil really is the New Testament, or whether two of their three contrasts are misquoted.

Any Muslim who raises those points is simply blind. An argument that cannot lose cannot be tested, and an argument that cannot be tested should not be trusted.

What the passages are about

The passages quoted also deserve to be read in context. John 12:40 quotes Isaiah Isa 6:9–10, and John applies it to people who had seen Jesus’ signs and still “did not believe in him” (John 12:37). The blindness in view is a refusal to accept Jesus as one sent by God despite what he did.

That does not describe Muslims. Muslims believe Jesus was sent by God.

They believe in his miraculous birth, his miracles of healing and raising the dead, by God’s permission Q 5:110, and his return. They honour him as the Messiah.

Muslims agree that God sent Jesus. They dispute whether Jesus is God and whether he died for the sins of the world.

Those are questions about doctrine, which Christians themselves debated for centuries before the councils settled them. Treating disagreement on them as satanic blindness turns a theological dispute into a spiritual accusation.

Paul’s words in Romans 1 are about people who “did not honour him as God or give thanks to him” and who “exchanged the glory of the immortal God for images” (Romans 1:21–23). Muslims, who refuse to make images of God, who pray to Him five times a day and who thank Him constantly, are among the least likely people on earth to fit that description.

The Qur’an’s way of inviting

The Qur’an takes a different approach to people who do not share its faith. It asks them to think.

“Do they not reflect on the Qur’an? If it were from other than God, they would have found much inconsistency in it” Q 4:82.

It asks for evidence and offers evidence. It tells Muslims to invite others “with wisdom and good instruction, and argue with them in the best way” Q 16:125. It forbids compulsion: “there is no compulsion in religion; the right way has become distinct from error” Q 2:256.

The Qur’an does speak of hearts that are sealed, but it describes that sealing as God’s response to persistent, knowing rejection, and it never gives Muslims the authority to diagnose it in a particular person. A Muslim who told a sincere Christian, “you cannot see the truth because God has sealed your heart”, would be claiming knowledge of another’s heart that the Qur’an reserves for God. Muslims should not use the blindness appeal against Christians, for the same reasons Christians should not use it against Muslims.

A better way to say it

There is a version of the page’s message that both Muslims and Christians can accept. Pride, fear, habit and the opinions of others can all keep a person from considering the truth fairly.

Anyone, of any faith, can be held back by them. The remedy is to read the sources honestly, to listen to the strongest case on the other side, and to ask God for guidance.

Muslims ask for that guidance in every unit of every prayer: “Guide us to the straight path” Q 1:6. That prayer is open to anyone.

A Christian who prays it sincerely keeps faith, and asks God, in whom they already believe, to show them the truth. The page itself recommends praying for God to open one’s eyes. Muslims would agree, and would add only that the prayer should be made without first deciding what the answer must be.

Why the appeal is tempting

It is worth asking why the blindness appeal is so common, in every religion. Part of the answer is that sincere believers find it hard to understand how anyone could see what they see and not believe. If the evidence seems overwhelming to me, and you remain unconvinced, the easiest explanation is that something is preventing you from seeing it.

That explanation is comforting, but it is rarely accurate. People disagree about religion for many reasons: they were raised differently, they find different arguments persuasive, they have read different sources, they have had different experiences.

Some are held back by pride or fear; many are not. A believer who takes seriously the possibility that the other person is sincere, intelligent and honest will have to argue harder.

That is a good thing. It forces both sides to look again at their evidence.

The Qur’an’s portrait of the prophets is instructive here. Noah preached to his people for centuries.

Abraham reasoned with his father and with the king. Moses argued with Pharaoh, showed him signs and answered his objections.

None of them simply told their audience that they were blind. They argued, they showed evidence, they appealed to reason and conscience, and they left the judgment of hearts to God.

A question for both sides

There is one question that both Muslims and Christians can usefully ask themselves when they are tempted to use the blindness appeal. If someone of the other faith said the same thing to me, would I find it persuasive, or would I find it insulting?

Most people, honestly answering, would find it insulting. That is a good reason not to say it to others.

The advice at the end

The page closes with three pieces of advice: pray, seek the truth by reading the Gospels and learning about Jesus, and do not harden your heart. Muslims can accept all three, and add a fourth.

Read the Gospels, and read the Qur’an alongside them, in a good translation, from the beginning. Read what the Qur’an says about Jesus in Sūrat Maryam and Sūrat Āl ʿImrān.

Ask which account of him best fits his own words in the Gospels: “the Lord our God, the Lord is one” Mark 12:29; “this is eternal life, that they know you, the only true God, and Jesus Christ whom you have sent” John 17:3. That is seeking the truth.

The same applies to this site. If our articles fail to persuade a Christian reader, the right conclusion is that we have not yet made our case well enough, or that the reader sees something we have missed. It is not that the reader is blind.

Conclusion

The spiritual blindness appeal explains disagreement without engaging it. It can be made by any faith against any other, it cannot be tested, and the passages it relies on describe people who rejected Jesus’ signs. Muslims honour him as the Messiah, and dispute only his divinity.

The Qur’an’s alternative is to ask for proof, invite reflection and forbid compulsion. Muslims should not answer the appeal by making it themselves. They should answer it by inviting the reader to compare the sources, and to pray for guidance without deciding the answer first.
